investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.front: What four analytes make up the bone profile?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.back:
• Calcium
  • phosphate
  • alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
  • and albumin
— the first-line panel for calcium and metabolic bone disorders.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.front: What is the corrected calcium formula and why is it needed?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.back: Corrected Ca (mmol/L) = measured Ca + 0.02 × (40 − albumin g/L). About half of calcium is albumin-bound, so a low albumin lowers the total without changing the active ionised level — correcting avoids missing true hypercalcaemia.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.front: A raised ALP could be bony or hepatic — how do you tell them apart?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.back: Check the GGT: a raised GGT points to a hepatic / cholestatic source; a normal GGT points to a bony source (Paget's, osteomalacia, bone mets, healing fracture). Bone-specific ALP can also be measured.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.front: Besides bone and liver disease, when is ALP physiologically raised?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.back: In growth (children/adolescents) and pregnancy (placental ALP) — so an isolated raised ALP is not always pathological.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.front: How does phosphate typically behave relative to calcium in PTH-driven disorders?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.back: PTH lowers phosphate (and raises calcium), so phosphate often moves opposite to calcium — e.g. primary hyperparathyroidism gives ↑Ca with ↓PO₄.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.front: What are the typical adult reference ranges for the bone profile?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.back:
• Adjusted calcium 2.20–2.60 mmol/L
  • phosphate 0.8–1.5 mmol/L
  • ALP 30–130 U/L
  • albumin 35–50 g/L
(check local lab).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.front: When should ionised calcium be measured directly rather than corrected?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.back: When accuracy is critical or albumin correction is unreliable — e.g. critical illness, acid–base disturbance, or massive transfusion (citrate binds calcium).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.front: Why must PTH always be interpreted relative to the calcium?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.back: PTH is only meaningful in context: a 'normal' PTH is inappropriate if the calcium is high (should be suppressed) or low (should be raised). Read the pair together.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.front: ↑ Calcium with a raised or inappropriately normal PTH — what is the diagnosis?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.back: Primary hyperparathyroidism (PTH failing to suppress). Also consider tertiary hyperPTH and familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (FHH).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.front: ↑ Calcium with a suppressed (low) PTH — what is the likely cause?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.back: Malignancy — PTHrP secretion or bone metastases — where the PTH is appropriately suppressed. Also vitamin D excess and granulomatous disease (sarcoidosis).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.front: ↓ Calcium with a raised PTH — what does this represent?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.back: Secondary hyperparathyroidism — an appropriate PTH response to vitamin D deficiency or CKD.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.front: ↓ Calcium with a low or inappropriately normal PTH — what is the diagnosis?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.back: Hypoparathyroidism (commonly post-surgical, or autoimmune). Also consider severe hypomagnesaemia (functional hypoparathyroidism).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.front: How does FHH differ from primary hyperparathyroidism, and why does it matter?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.back: Both give ↑Ca with ↑/normal PTH, but FHH has a LOW urine calcium (low calcium:creatinine clearance ratio). It is benign — recognising it avoids unnecessary parathyroid surgery.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.front: Why can hypocalcaemia be refractory to calcium replacement?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.back: Severe hypomagnesaemia causes functional hypoparathyroidism — the calcium will not correct until the magnesium is replaced.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.front: What does the bone profile look like in osteoporosis, and how is it diagnosed?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.back: The bone profile is completely normal (Ca, PO₄, ALP, PTH). Osteoporosis is diagnosed on DEXA: T-score ≤ −2.5 (−1 to −2.5 = osteopenia). Bloods are done to exclude secondary causes.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.front: What is the biochemical pattern of osteomalacia / rickets?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.back: ↓Ca · ↓PO₄ · ↑ALP · ↑PTH with a low vitamin D — the secondary-hyperparathyroidism picture. Look for proximal myopathy and Looser's zones on X-ray.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.front: What is the classic bone profile of Paget's disease of bone?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.back: An isolated, often very high ALP with normal calcium and phosphate. Clinically: bone pain, bowing, skull enlargement, deafness.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.front: What is the bone profile pattern in CKD–mineral bone disorder (renal osteodystrophy)?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.back: ↓Ca · ↑PO₄ · ↑ALP · ↑↑PTH — the key exception where phosphate is HIGH (the failing kidney cannot excrete it), driving secondary/tertiary hyperparathyroidism.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.front: Why does multiple myeloma classically have a NORMAL ALP despite extensive bone destruction?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.back: Myeloma lesions are purely osteoclastic (lytic) with no osteoblastic response, so ALP (an osteoblast marker) stays normal — unlike bone metastases or Paget's. Calcium is often raised.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.front: Which metabolic bone disease has a completely normal bone profile — and what tool estimates fracture risk?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.back: Osteoporosis (normal Ca/PO₄/ALP/PTH). Fracture risk is estimated with FRAX (or QFracture); the diagnosis itself is by DEXA T-score.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.front: What is the bone profile of primary hyperparathyroidism?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.back: ↑Ca · ↓PO₄ · ↑PTH (± raised ALP if there is bone disease / osteitis fibrosa cystica).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.front: How is osteomalacia / vitamin D deficiency treated, and what confirms response?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.back: Vitamin D replacement (colecalciferol, ± calcium). Recheck the bone profile — calcium and phosphate rise, ALP and PTH settle as bone remineralises. Correct any underlying cause (malabsorption, CKD).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: What does the U&E measure and what does it assess?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back: Sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine (± bicarbonate). It assesses renal function, hydration, electrolyte and acid–base status.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: Serum sodium is primarily a marker of what?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back: Water balance, not salt content — hypo/hypernatraemia usually reflect too much or too little water relative to sodium.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: What does a raised urea:creatinine ratio (urea up out of proportion) suggest?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back: A pre-renal picture — dehydration/hypovolaemia — or an upper GI bleed (absorbed blood protein raises urea).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: Why can creatinine be misleading as a marker of renal function?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back: It depends on muscle mass — it can be falsely low in the frail, elderly or cachectic (masking poor GFR) and higher in muscular people.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: List common causes of hyperkalaemia and its ECG changes.
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back:
• AKI/CKD
  • K⁺-sparing diuretics
  • ACEi/ARB
  • Addison's
  • acidosis
  • or a haemolysed sample
ECG: tall tented T waves → flattened P → widened QRS → sine wave.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: Outline the emergency management of severe hyperkalaemia.
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back: IV calcium gluconate (cardioprotection — does not lower K⁺), then insulin + dextrose and nebulised salbutamol to shift K⁺ into cells; treat the cause (± potassium binder / dialysis).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: Give causes of hypokalaemia and its ECG changes.
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back:
• GI loss (vomiting/diarrhoea)
  • diuretics
  • Conn's syndrome
  • alkalosis
ECG: flat T waves and U waves.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: How is eGFR estimated, and how is it reported?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back: From creatinine with age and sex (CKD-EPI, race-free equation), reported per 1.73 m².

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: In which situations is eGFR unreliable?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back: In AKI (creatinine not in steady state), extremes of muscle mass, pregnancy and acute illness — follow the creatinine trend instead.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: What defines chronic kidney disease (CKD)?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back: GFR <60 or markers of kidney damage (ACR ≥3, haematuria, structural/histological abnormality) persisting for ≥3 months.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: How is CKD staged, and what do the G and A categories mean?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back: By GFR (G1–G5: ≥90, 60–89, 45–59, 30–44, 15–29, <15) and albuminuria (A1–A3: ACR <3, 3–30, >30 mg/mmol). Higher G+A = greater risk.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: What is the preferred test for albuminuria in CKD?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back: The urine albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR) — more sensitive and standardised than protein:creatinine ratio for early kidney damage.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: Give key criteria for nephrology referral in CKD.
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back:
• eGFR <30 (G4–5)
  • ACR ≥70
  • ACR ≥30 with haematuria
  • a rapid decline in eGFR
  • or suspected genetic/rare cause

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: State the KDIGO criteria for diagnosing AKI (any one).
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back:
• Creatinine rise ≥26 µmol/L within 48 h
  • or creatinine ≥1.5× baseline within 7 days
  • or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥6 h

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: How is AKI staged 1–3 by creatinine?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back:
• Stage 1: 1.5–1.9× baseline (or ≥26 rise)
  • Stage 2: 2.0–2.9×
  • Stage 3: ≥3× (or ≥354 µmol/L) or need for RRT

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: Give the three categories of AKI cause with examples.
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back:
• Pre-renal (commonest): hypovolaemia, sepsis, hypotension, NSAIDs/ACEi
  • Intrinsic: ATN, glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis, vasculitis
  • Post-renal: obstruction (stones, prostate, tumour)

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: What are the key management principles of AKI?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back:
• Restore volume and treat the cause (esp. sepsis)
  • stop nephrotoxics (NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB, gentamicin, contrast)
  • catheterise/ultrasound to exclude obstruction
  • monitor K⁺, fluids and acid–base

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: What are the indications for urgent dialysis in AKI?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back:
AEIOU refractory to medical therapy:
  • Acidosis (severe)
  • Electrolytes (refractory hyperkalaemia)
  • Intoxication
  • Overload (pulmonary oedema)
  • Uraemia (encephalopathy/pericarditis)

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: Which single investigation must not be missed in AKI to exclude a post-renal cause?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back: A renal tract ultrasound — to exclude obstruction (hydronephrosis), which is reversible with catheterisation/nephrostomy.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: Serum sodium disorders are fundamentally disorders of what — and what is the pivot of the work-up?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back: Disorders of water balance. The pivot is volume status (assessed alongside serum/urine osmolality and urine sodium).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: What are the diagnostic features of SIADH?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with a low serum osmolality but inappropriately concentrated urine (osm >100, urine Na >30), and normal thyroid and adrenal function.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: Give common causes and the first-line treatment of SIADH.
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back:
Causes:
  • CNS disease
  • lung (small-cell) cancer
  • drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine)
  • surgery/pain
Treatment: fluid restriction and treat the cause.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: What is the safe rate of correction for hyponatraemia, and why does it matter?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back: Raise the sodium by no more than ~8–10 mmol/L in 24 h (less if high-risk). Faster correction risks osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: How is severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures/reduced GCS) treated?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back: Hypertonic (3%) saline in small boluses under senior/critical-care guidance, with frequent sodium monitoring to avoid overcorrection.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: Hypernatraemia always represents what, and how is it corrected?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back: A water deficit (poor intake, D&V, osmotic diuresis, diabetes insipidus). Replace water slowly (~10 mmol/L/24 h) to avoid cerebral oedema.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: List common causes of a raised serum urate.
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back:
• Gout
  • tumour lysis syndrome
  • CKD
  • thiazide/loop diuretics
  • alcohol/high purine intake
  • myeloproliferative disorders
  • and pre-eclampsia

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: Why can a normal serum urate not exclude acute gout?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back: Urate often falls to normal (or low) during an acute attack. Diagnose on the joint aspirate (negatively birefringent needle-shaped MSU crystals) and recheck urate 4–6 weeks later.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: What is the biochemical picture of tumour lysis syndrome?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back: ↑ urate, ↑ potassium, ↑ phosphate and ↓ calcium — risking AKI and arrhythmia. Prevent with hydration/allopurinol; treat with rasburicase.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: What is the rule about treating asymptomatic hyperuricaemia, and when is urate-lowering therapy indicated?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back: Do not treat asymptomatic hyperuricaemia. Start urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol) for recurrent gout, tophi or urate stones — after the attack settles, under prophylactic cover.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: A patient has a hot, swollen joint and a raised urate. What must be excluded before assuming gout?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back: Septic arthritis — always aspirate the joint for crystals AND Gram stain/culture; a raised urate does not confirm gout, and a normal one does not exclude it.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.front: How is hypokalaemia managed, and what electrolyte must you also check?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.back: Replace potassium — oral if mild; IV (max ~10 mmol/h peripherally) if K⁺ <3.0 or symptomatic/arrhythmic (cardiac-monitored; central line for faster rates). Always check and replace magnesium — low Mg²⁺ causes refractory hypokalaemia — and treat the cause.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: Which LFT enzymes indicate hepatocellular vs cholestatic disease?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back: Hepatocellular: ALT & AST (ALT more liver-specific). Cholestatic: ALP & GGT. A hepatocellular pattern has ALT/AST rise > ALP; a cholestatic pattern has ALP/GGT rise > ALT.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: How do you tell whether a raised ALP is from liver or bone?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back: Check the GGT: a raised GGT points to a hepatic/cholestatic source; a normal GGT suggests a bony source of the ALP.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: What AST:ALT ratio suggests alcoholic liver disease?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back: An AST:ALT ratio >2 is suggestive of alcohol (AST is disproportionately raised).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: Distinguish unconjugated from conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back: Unconjugated (pre-hepatic) — haemolysis or Gilbert's; not water-soluble, so no bilirubinuria. Conjugated — hepatic/post-hepatic; obstructive causes dark urine and pale stools.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: What is Gilbert's syndrome and its biochemical signature?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back: A benign inherited defect of bilirubin conjugation → an isolated raised unconjugated bilirubin with otherwise normal LFTs, worse with fasting or intercurrent illness. No treatment needed.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: Which LFT components reflect the liver's synthetic function?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back: Albumin (falls in chronic disease) and the PT/INR (prolongs in acute or severe injury) — the standard enzymes (ALT/ALP) reflect damage, not function.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: What defines acute liver failure and what is the commonest UK cause?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back: Jaundice + coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5) + encephalopathy. The commonest UK cause is paracetamol overdose — treat with N-acetylcysteine and discuss with a liver unit.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: How do amylase and lipase compare in diagnosing acute pancreatitis?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back: Lipase is more sensitive and specific and stays raised longer (better for late presentation). Amylase rises early but falls within 24–48 h and is less specific. Either >3× ULN supports the diagnosis.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: What are the diagnostic criteria for acute pancreatitis?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back:
Two of three:
  • (1) characteristic epigastric pain radiating to the back
  • (2) amylase/lipase >3× upper limit
  • (3) characteristic CT findings

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: Does the height of the amylase reflect the severity of pancreatitis?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back: No. The enzyme level does not correlate with severity — use a validated score (Glasgow / APACHE II) and CRP instead.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: Give non-pancreatic causes of a raised amylase.
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back:
• Bowel perforation or ischaemia
  • ectopic pregnancy
  • DKA
  • parotitis (salivary)
  • macroamylasaemia
  • and renal failure
In late/alcoholic/hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis, amylase may be normal — use lipase.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: What are the two commonest causes of acute pancreatitis, and the mnemonic?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back: Gallstones and alcohol. Mnemonic GET SMASHED (Gallstones, Ethanol, Trauma, Steroids, Mumps, Autoimmune, Scorpion, Hypertriglyceridaemia/Hypercalcaemia, ERCP, Drugs).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: How is ammonia metabolised, and why is it clinically important?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back: It is a product of protein metabolism/gut bacteria, detoxified by the liver's urea cycle. It crosses the blood–brain barrier and is neurotoxic → encephalopathy.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: In which settings is a serum ammonia measured?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back:
• Hepatic encephalopathy (cirrhosis/ALF)
  • unexplained encephalopathy or coma, especially in neonates/children (urea cycle disorders, organic acidaemias)
  • and valproate toxicity

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: What are the sample-handling requirements for ammonia?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back: Send on ice and analyse quickly — delay, haemolysis or a tourniquet cause a falsely raised result.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: Does the ammonia level correlate with the grade of hepatic encephalopathy?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back: No — poorly. Hepatic encephalopathy is a clinical diagnosis; ammonia is supportive, not diagnostic. In known cirrhosis it is not routinely needed to diagnose HE.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: Outline the management of hepatic encephalopathy.
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back: Treat precipitants (infection, GI bleed, constipation, electrolyte disturbance, sedatives), and give lactulose ± rifaximin to reduce gut ammonia.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: What is the physiological role of α₁-antitrypsin?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back: A liver-made antiprotease that inhibits neutrophil elastase, protecting tissues — especially the lung — from proteolytic damage.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: What are the two organ manifestations of α₁-antitrypsin deficiency?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back:
• Lung: early-onset, basal-predominant emphysema (unopposed elastase, worse in smokers)
  • Liver: neonatal hepatitis and adult cirrhosis/HCC from accumulation of misfolded protein

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: Why does α₁-antitrypsin deficiency cause liver disease?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back: The abnormal PiZZ protein misfolds and accumulates within hepatocytes (a gain-of-function/retention injury) — causing hepatitis, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: How is α₁-antitrypsin deficiency diagnosed, and what is the pitfall?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back: Serum A1AT level (low) — but it is an acute-phase reactant, so it can be falsely normal in inflammation (check CRP). Confirm with Pi typing: PiMM normal, PiZZ severe, PiMZ carrier.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: What is the single most important management step in α₁-antitrypsin deficiency?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back: Smoking cessation — smoking dramatically accelerates the emphysema. Also manage COPD, monitor the liver, screen family; augmentation therapy in selected cases.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: What is the classic biochemical/ophthalmic triad of Wilson's disease?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back:
• Low caeruloplasmin
  • high 24-hour urinary copper
  • and Kayser–Fleischer rings (copper in Descemet's membrane on slit-lamp)

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: Why can a normal caeruloplasmin not exclude Wilson's disease?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back: Caeruloplasmin is an acute-phase reactant — it can be falsely normal during inflammation, pregnancy or oestrogen use. Interpret with the other tests.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: What happens to total vs free serum copper in Wilson's disease?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back: Total serum copper is often low (less caeruloplasmin to carry it), but the free (non-caeruloplasmin) copper is HIGH — the toxic fraction that deposits in tissues.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: Who should be tested for Wilson's disease?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back: A young patient (<40) with unexplained liver disease (hepatitis/cirrhosis/ALF), and anyone with unexplained neuropsychiatric features (tremor, dystonia, parkinsonism, psychiatric change).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: How is Wilson's disease treated?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back: Copper chelation with penicillamine or trientine, plus zinc (blocks gut absorption); lifelong, with a low-copper diet. Liver transplant for fulminant/advanced disease.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: What biochemical clues suggest Wilson's disease presenting as acute liver failure?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back: A low ALP, a Coombs-negative haemolytic anaemia and a high bilirubin (a low ALP:bilirubin ratio) — a rapidly fatal presentation needing urgent transplant.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: Cholestatic LFTs (↑↑ALP/GGT) — what is the immediate next investigation?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back:
An abdominal ultrasound of the liver and biliary tree.
  • Dilated ducts = extrahepatic obstruction (stone/tumour) → MRCP/ERCP
  • non-dilated ducts = intrahepatic cholestasis (PBC, PSC, drugs, infiltration)

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.front: Unexplained deranged hepatocellular LFTs — what 'non-invasive liver screen' do you send?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.back:
• Viral hepatitis serology (B, C)
  • autoantibodies (ANA, SMA, AMA, anti-LKM) + immunoglobulins
  • ferritin + transferrin saturation (haemochromatosis)
  • caeruloplasmin (Wilson's)
  • α₁-antitrypsin level
  • ± coeliac serology and TFTs
  • and fasting lipids/glucose for NAFLD

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.front: What does HbA1c reflect, and what is its diagnostic threshold for diabetes?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.back: Average glycaemia over ~8–12 weeks (red-cell lifespan); no fasting needed. ≥48 mmol/mol (6.5%) diagnoses diabetes.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.front: List the glucose-based diagnostic thresholds for diabetes.
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.back:
• Fasting glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L
  • 2-h OGTT or random ≥11.1 mmol/L (random requires symptoms)

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.front: How many abnormal tests are needed to diagnose diabetes?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.back: If symptomatic, one abnormal result suffices. If asymptomatic, you need two abnormal results (repeat to confirm).

• HbA1c 42–47 mmol/mol
  • impaired fasting glucose 6.1–6.9
  • impaired glucose tolerance (2-h 7.8–11.0 on OGTT)

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.front: How often is HbA1c checked for monitoring, and what is a typical target?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.back: Every 3–6 months; individualised targets around 48–58 mmol/mol, with capillary glucose/CGM for day-to-day control.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.front: In which conditions is HbA1c falsely LOW?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.back:
Those that shorten red-cell lifespan / raise turnover:
  • haemolysis
  • recent blood loss or transfusion
  • pregnancy
  • reticulocytosis
  • splenomegaly

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.front: In which conditions is HbA1c falsely HIGH?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.back: Those that lengthen red-cell lifespan: untreated iron, B12 or folate deficiency anaemia, and splenectomy.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.front: When should HbA1c NOT be used to diagnose diabetes at all?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.back: In pregnancy, suspected type 1 (rapid onset/children), acute illness, pancreatic damage, steroids, and haemoglobinopathies (HbS/HbC interfere) — use glucose criteria instead.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.front: What alternative test reflects shorter-term glycaemic control when HbA1c is unreliable?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.back: Fructosamine (glycated albumin), which reflects the previous ~2–3 weeks.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.front: How does iron-deficiency anaemia affect the HbA1c?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.back: It raises the HbA1c (longer red-cell lifespan) — potentially overestimating control or overdiagnosing diabetes; recheck after treating the anaemia or use glucose.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.front: What does C-peptide indicate, and how does it differ between diabetes types?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.back: It is co-secreted 1:1 with insulin → a marker of endogenous insulin. Low/undetectable in type 1 (beta-cell failure); preserved/high in type 2 or MODY.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.front: What do positive GAD or IA-2 antibodies indicate?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.back: Autoimmune (type 1) diabetes — or LADA (latent autoimmune diabetes in adults) when it presents in an adult initially labelled type 2.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.front: What features suggest MODY, and how is it confirmed?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.back:
• Young onset
  • strong family history
  • preserved C-peptide
  • and negative autoantibodies
→ confirm with genetic testing.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.front: In a hypoglycaemia work-up, how do insulin and C-peptide distinguish the cause?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.back:
• High insulin + high C-peptide = endogenous (insulinoma or sulfonylurea)
  • High insulin + low C-peptide = exogenous insulin administration
Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults — a slowly-progressive autoimmune (antibody-positive) diabetes that presents in adulthood and is often initially misdiagnosed as type 2.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.front: An acutely unwell patient has a high glucose. Why is HbA1c not the test to reach for, and what should you do?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes &.back: HbA1c reflects the last ~3 months and won't guide an acute emergency. In an unwell hyperglycaemic patient check blood/capillary ketones and a venous blood gas to identify DKA (ketones + acidosis) or HHS (marked hyperglycaemia/dehydration, no ketosis) — both are emergencies.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.front: What are the kinetics of cardiac troponin after myocardial injury?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.back:
• Rises at 3–6 h
  • peaks at 12–24 h
  • and stays elevated for days
High-sensitivity assays detect very small, early rises.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.front: How is myocardial infarction defined (4th Universal Definition)?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.back: A rise and/or fall of troponin with at least one value >99th percentile, PLUS evidence of ischaemia (symptoms, ischaemic ECG changes, or imaging). Troponin alone = injury, not MI.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.front: Give non-ACS causes of a raised troponin.
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.back:
• Type 2 MI (supply-demand: sepsis, tachyarrhythmia, anaemia, hypotension)
  • PE
  • heart failure
  • myocarditis
  • CKD (reduced clearance)
  • post-cardiac-arrest
  • aortic dissection

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.front: What distinguishes type 1 from type 2 MI?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.back:
• Type 1 = an atherothrombotic (plaque rupture) coronary event
  • Type 2 = a supply–demand mismatch (e.g. sepsis, tachyarrhythmia, anaemia, hypotension) without acute plaque rupture

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.front: Why is a single static raised troponin interpreted differently from a dynamic one?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.back: A dynamic rise/fall on serial testing suggests acute injury (e.g. MI); a static elevation without ischaemia is often chronic (CKD, structural heart disease).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.front: What is the role of CK-MB now that troponin is standard?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.back: Largely superseded (less specific — also skeletal muscle), but CK-MB falls faster, so it can help detect re-infarction shortly after an index MI.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.front: How do the ESC 0/1-hour (and 0/3-hour) hs-troponin pathways triage chest pain?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.back:
Using a baseline troponin plus the delta (change):
  • very low/no change → rule out
  • high or a significant rise → rule in
  • in-between → observe and repeat at 3 h

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.front: Why does the delta (change) matter as much as the absolute troponin value?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.back: A dynamic rise/fall indicates acute myocardial injury; a stable elevation may be chronic. In chronically elevated patients (CKD) you rely on the delta, not the absolute level.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.front: What must accompany hs-troponin interpretation in a chest-pain pathway?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.back: The ECG and a clinical risk score (e.g. HEART). Thresholds are assay-specific (hs-cTnT ≠ cTnI) and the 99th percentile is sex-specific.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.front: What is the pitfall of a single troponin in very early presentation?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.back: Within ~1–2 h of pain onset troponin may not yet have risen, so a single low value can miss an MI — repeat the troponin.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.front: With high-sensitivity troponin, how are unstable angina and NSTEMI distinguished?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.back: Unstable angina = ischaemic symptoms with a normal troponin (no rise); a troponin rise/fall reclassifies it as NSTEMI.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.front: What triggers BNP/NT-proBNP release, and what is their main clinical value?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.back: Release from ventricular myocardium in response to wall stretch/stress. Their main value is as a rule-out test for heart failure — a normal level makes HF unlikely (high NPV).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.front: Give the NICE NT-proBNP thresholds for suspected (chronic) heart failure.
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.back:
• <400 ng/L → HF unlikely
  • 400–2000 → echo within 6 weeks
  • >2000 → urgent referral + echo within 2 weeks (worse prognosis)

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.front: What non-heart-failure factors raise BNP/NT-proBNP?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.back:
• Older age
  • AF
  • renal impairment (reduced clearance)
  • PE
  • sepsis
  • LVH and valve disease
— so a raised level is non-specific.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.front: What effect does obesity have on BNP, and why does it matter?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.back: Obesity lowers BNP — a 'normal' level can be falsely reassuring in an obese patient (including HFpEF); interpret with caution.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.front: How does sacubitril/valsartan (ARNI) affect natriuretic peptides?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.back: Neprilysin inhibition blocks BNP breakdown, so BNP rises; NT-proBNP is not a neprilysin substrate, so monitor with NT-proBNP in patients on an ARNI.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.front: What is the modern treatment target in the lipid profile, and is fasting required?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.back: Non-HDL cholesterol (total − HDL) — it captures all atherogenic particles. Fasting is not required for most lipid samples.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.front: What is the primary-prevention statin rule based on CV risk?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.back: A QRISK3 ≥10% (10-year CV risk) → offer atorvastatin 20 mg. (Also treat qualifying type 1 diabetes and CKD.)

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.front: What is the secondary-prevention statin regimen and target?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.back: Established CVD → atorvastatin 80 mg (high-intensity); aim for a ≥40% reduction in non-HDL cholesterol, rechecked at 3 months (add ezetimibe ± PCSK9 inhibitor if not met).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.front: What features suggest familial hypercholesterolaemia?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.back:
• Very high LDL/total cholesterol
  • tendon xanthomata
  • and a family history of premature cardiovascular disease
→ specialist referral and cascade screening of relatives.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.front: What is the danger of very high triglycerides (>10 mmol/L)?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.back: Acute pancreatitis. Treat with a fibrate and lifestyle change, and look for secondary causes (alcohol, diabetes, obesity, hypothyroidism).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.front: How are statins monitored for safety (liver and muscle)?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Ma.back: Check baseline LFTs before starting, then recheck at 3 and 12 months — only stop if transaminases rise >3× the upper limit of normal. Check CK only if the patient has muscle symptoms (not routinely).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.front: Why is TSH the first-line thyroid test, and how is it interpreted?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.back: TSH is the most sensitive marker of thyroid status (log-inverse relationship with T4). Interpret it together with free T4.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.front: Give the TFT patterns for hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism and their subclinical forms.
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.back:
• ↓TSH + ↑fT4 = primary hyperthyroid
  • ↑TSH + ↓fT4 = primary hypothyroid
  • ↑TSH + normal fT4 = subclinical hypothyroid
  • ↓TSH + normal fT4 = subclinical hyperthyroid

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.front: Which thyroid antibodies are useful, and in what conditions?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.back:
• TPO antibodies — Hashimoto's and Graves'
  • TSH-receptor antibodies (TRAb) — Graves' disease

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.front: What is sick euthyroid syndrome, and its implication for testing?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.back: Abnormal TFTs during non-thyroidal (acute) illness. Don't test thyroid function in acute illness — repeat once the patient has recovered.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.front: How does central (secondary) hypothyroidism present biochemically, and why is it a trap?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.back: A low free T4 with an inappropriately normal or low TSH (pituitary/hypothalamic disease). Relying on TSH alone would miss it — check fT4.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.front: Name the two thyroid emergencies.
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.back:
• Thyroid storm (severe thyrotoxicosis: fever, tachyarrhythmia, agitation)
  • and myxoedema coma (severe hypothyroidism: hypothermia, reduced GCS)

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.front: Who should be screened for secondary (endocrine) hypertension?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.back:
• The young (<40)
  • resistant (≥3 drugs)
  • severe/accelerated hypertensive
  • those with hypokalaemia
  • or with suggestive clinical features

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.front: Which test screens for primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's), and what is the classic picture?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.back: The aldosterone:renin ratio (ARR) — a raised ratio. Classic: hypertension with hypokalaemia and alkalosis (though often normokalaemic).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.front: Which test screens for phaeochromocytoma, and what are the symptoms?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.back: Plasma or 24-hour urine metanephrines. Symptoms: episodic headache, sweating, palpitations with paroxysmal hypertension.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.front: How is Cushing's syndrome screened for biochemically?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.back:
• Overnight (1 mg) dexamethasone suppression test
  • late-night salivary cortisol
  • or 24-hour urinary free cortisol
— failure to suppress suggests Cushing's.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.front: What is the critical drug-safety rule in phaeochromocytoma?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.back: Alpha-blockade before beta-blockade — giving a beta-blocker first leaves unopposed alpha stimulation and can precipitate a hypertensive crisis.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.front: Why is IGF-1, not a random growth hormone, used to screen for acromegaly?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.back: GH secretion is pulsatile (varies widely), so a random GH is unreliable. IGF-1 (liver-derived, GH-driven) is stable and integrates GH over time — the screening test.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.front: How is acromegaly confirmed after a raised IGF-1?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.back: An oral glucose tolerance test with GH measurement: glucose normally suppresses GH, but in acromegaly GH fails to suppress. Then a pituitary MRI to find the adenoma.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.front: List clinical features that should prompt testing for acromegaly.
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.back:
• Acral enlargement (hands/feet)
  • jaw prognathism and coarse features
  • sweating
  • headaches
  • bitemporal hemianopia
  • carpal tunnel
  • and complications (diabetes, hypertension, OSA, colon polyps)

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.front: What is the first-line treatment for acromegaly, and the medical options?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.back:
Trans-sphenoidal surgery is first-line. Medical options:
  • somatostatin analogues (octreotide/lanreotide)
  • the GH-receptor antagonist pegvisomant
  • and cabergoline
Monitor with IGF-1.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.front: In which physiological states is IGF-1 normally elevated?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.back: Puberty/adolescence and pregnancy — interpret IGF-1 against age- and sex-specific reference ranges.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.front: What is serum ACE and its role in sarcoidosis?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.back: An enzyme produced by the epithelioid cells of granulomas. In sarcoidosis it is a supportive, non-diagnostic marker — mainly used to monitor disease activity.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.front: Why can serum ACE neither diagnose nor exclude sarcoidosis?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.back: It is raised in only ~60% (so a normal level doesn't exclude it) and is non-specific — also raised in TB, leprosy, histoplasmosis, hyperthyroidism, diabetes and silicosis.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.front: How is sarcoidosis actually diagnosed?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.back: Clinically + radiologically + histologically — classically non-caseating granulomas on biopsy, with a CXR showing bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.front: What causes hypercalcaemia in sarcoidosis?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.back: Macrophages in granulomas produce 1,25-(OH)₂ vitamin D (active vitamin D), increasing gut calcium absorption. Hypercalciuria is even more common than hypercalcaemia.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.front: What drug interferes with serum ACE measurement?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.back: ACE inhibitors lower the serum ACE level (they inhibit the enzyme being measured).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.front: How do you manage subclinical hypothyroidism (↑TSH, normal fT4)?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.back:
Repeat the TSH in ~3 months to confirm it persists. Treat with levothyroxine if
  • TSH ≥10 mU/L
  • or if symptomatic
  • TPO-antibody positive
  • or pregnant/planning pregnancy
Otherwise monitor.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.front: A Cushing's screen (e.g. failed overnight dexamethasone suppression) is positive — what is the next biochemical step?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.back: Measure ACTH to split ACTH-dependent (pituitary Cushing's disease / ectopic) from ACTH-independent (adrenal tumour), then refer for localisation.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.front: How is a raised aldosterone:renin ratio (screening positive for Conn's) confirmed?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine.back: With a saline / salt-loading suppression test — aldosterone fails to suppress — then CT adrenals (± specialist referral). Stop interfering antihypertensives before testing where possible.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.front: What is the golden rule for using tumour markers?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.back: They are for monitoring treatment response and detecting recurrence in a known cancer — not for screening asymptomatic people or diagnosing cancer (poor sensitivity/specificity).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.front: Which cancers raise CA19-9, and what benign conditions also raise it?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.back: Pancreatic and biliary (cholangiocarcinoma) cancers. Also raised (benign) in obstructive jaundice/cholestasis, pancreatitis and cirrhosis — recheck after biliary drainage.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.front: Why can CA19-9 be falsely normal in some patients?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.back: About 5–10% of people are Lewis-antigen-negative and do not secrete CA19-9, so it stays normal even with disease.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.front: What cancer is CEA used to monitor, and what is its role?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.back: Colorectal cancer — to monitor for recurrence after resection, not to screen or diagnose. It is non-specific (also raised by smoking, IBD, pancreatitis).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.front: What is used for bowel-cancer screening, if not CEA?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.back: FIT (faecal immunochemical test) and colonoscopy — CEA is not a screening test.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.front: What is AFP used for in liver disease, and what is the surveillance protocol?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.back: It is raised in hepatocellular carcinoma. HCC surveillance in cirrhosis / chronic hepatitis B is 6-monthly ultrasound ± AFP — ultrasound is the mainstay (AFP alone lacks sensitivity).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.front: Besides HCC, what raises AFP?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.back:
• Non-seminomatous germ-cell (yolk-sac) tumours
  • pregnancy (physiological; also a fetal screening marker)
  • and active hepatitis/liver regeneration (modest)

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.front: How is a raised AFP interpreted in a cirrhotic patient?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.back: A markedly raised or rising AFP with a liver lesion → HCC (classic contrast CT/MRI may be diagnostic without biopsy). Modest rises are non-specific — use the trend + imaging.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.front: Does a raised AFP occur in pure seminoma?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.back: No. A raised AFP indicates a non-seminomatous element (yolk-sac/embryonal); pure seminoma does not raise AFP — a key discriminator.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.front: Why does HCC surveillance matter in cirrhosis?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.back: Structured surveillance detects HCC early when it is still curable — improving survival in this high-risk group.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.front: Besides prostate cancer, what raises PSA?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.back:
• BPH
  • prostatitis/UTI
  • urinary retention
  • catheterisation
  • DRE
  • ejaculation
  • and vigorous exercise/cycling
— PSA is organ-specific, not cancer-specific.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.front: What practical timing rules apply to PSA testing?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.back: Check PSA before a DRE, and defer testing after a recent UTI, ejaculation or catheterisation (all transiently raise it).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.front: How does the free:total PSA ratio help?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.back: Cancer binds more PSA, so a LOW free:total ratio favours malignancy; a high ratio favours benign BPH.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.front: What do PSA density and PSA velocity indicate?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.back:
• PSA density = PSA ÷ prostate volume (higher favours cancer)
  • PSA velocity = rate of rise / doubling time (a rapid rise favours cancer)

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.front: What is the current pathway for a raised PSA?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.back: Refer (2-week wait) → multiparametric MRI then targeted biopsy. Screening is controversial (no national programme) — a shared, informed decision.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.front: What does a rising PSA after prostate cancer treatment indicate?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.back: Recurrence. After radical prostatectomy the PSA should be undetectable, so any detectable/rising value signals recurrence.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.front: Which three markers are used for testicular germ-cell tumours, and what does each reflect?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.back:
• AFP (non-seminomatous / yolk-sac)
  • β-hCG (trophoblastic — choriocarcinoma, some seminomas)
  • and LDH (tumour bulk/turnover, for staging/prognosis)

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.front: What is the key discriminator that AFP provides in testicular tumours?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.back: A raised AFP means NON-seminomatous disease — even if the histology looks like seminoma, an elevated AFP means it is managed as a non-seminomatous germ-cell tumour (NSGCT). Pure seminoma does NOT raise AFP.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.front: What can a very high β-hCG cause clinically?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.back: Gynaecomastia (and rarely thyrotoxicosis, via cross-reactivity of hCG with the TSH receptor). β-hCG is high in choriocarcinoma and ~15–20% of seminomas.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.front: How are testicular tumour markers used in staging and monitoring?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.back: Measured before and after orchidectomy; post-orchidectomy levels define the S category of TNM staging. Half-lives (AFP ~5–7 days, β-hCG ~24–36 h) are tracked — failure to fall suggests residual/metastatic disease.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.front: What must NOT be done to a suspicious testicular mass, and what is done instead?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Mar.back: Do NOT biopsy the testis (risk of tumour seeding). Perform a radical inguinal orchidectomy (diagnostic and therapeutic) after ultrasound and markers.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.front: How do CRP and procalcitonin differ as inflammatory markers?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.back: CRP is a sensitive but non-specific acute-phase protein (rises in any inflammation). Procalcitonin is more specific for bacterial infection/sepsis and rises faster.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.front: What is procalcitonin mainly used for clinically?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.back: To help distinguish bacterial from viral infection and to guide antibiotic stewardship — PCT-guided stopping safely shortens antibiotic courses.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.front: Give non-infective causes of a raised CRP.
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.back:
• Surgery
  • myocardial infarction
  • trauma
  • malignancy
  • and autoimmune disease
— CRP is not specific to infection.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.front: In whom might a normal CRP be falsely reassuring?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.back: The immunosuppressed and elderly can mount a blunted CRP response, so a normal level does not exclude serious infection.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.front: Should you wait for CRP/procalcitonin before treating suspected sepsis?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.back: No. Sepsis is a clinical diagnosis — deliver the Sepsis 6 within 1 hour; the markers support and trend but do not diagnose it.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.front: What does a raised lactate indicate, and what are the key thresholds?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.back: Tissue hypoperfusion / anaerobic metabolism. >2 mmol/L is abnormal; >4 mmol/L is severe (a marker of shock and worse prognosis).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.front: Distinguish type A from type B lactic acidosis with examples.
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.back:
• Type A (hypoxic): inadequate O₂ delivery — sepsis, shock, cardiac arrest, bowel/limb ischaemia
  • Type B (non-hypoxic): liver failure, metformin, DKA, thiamine deficiency, malignancy, seizures, salbutamol, alcohol

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.front: How is lactate used in sepsis, and what does clearance signify?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.back: It is part of the Sepsis 6; a lactate >2 (especially >4) signals severity → aggressive fluids. Lactate clearance (a falling level) is a good prognostic sign; persistent/rising lactate is ominous.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.front: What sampling factors can falsely raise a lactate?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.back:
• A tourniquet
  • delayed sample processing
  • and using a venous rather than arterial sample (venous is acceptable for screening but arterial is more accurate)

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.front: What drug classically causes a type B lactic acidosis, especially in renal impairment?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.back: Metformin — metformin-associated lactic acidosis, particularly when it accumulates in AKI/CKD.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.front: What is the mechanism of refeeding syndrome?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.back: Reintroducing carbohydrate to a starved patient causes an insulin surge → cells take up phosphate, potassium and magnesium → plasma levels fall sharply. Hypophosphataemia is the hallmark.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.front: Why is hypophosphataemia in refeeding dangerous?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.back: It causes cardiac arrhythmias, cardiac/respiratory failure, rhabdomyolysis and seizures — refeeding syndrome can be fatal.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.front: Who is at high risk of refeeding syndrome (NICE)?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.back:
• Little/no intake >10 days
  • BMI <16
  • unintentional weight loss >15%
  • low baseline K/PO₄/Mg
  • and alcohol/drug misuse or chemotherapy

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.front: How is refeeding syndrome prevented and managed?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.back:
• Check phosphate, potassium, magnesium before and daily
  • start feeding slowly (~10 kcal/kg/day) and increase gradually
  • replace electrolytes and give thiamine (Pabrinex) before/with feeding

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.front: Why is thiamine given before refeeding?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.back: Carbohydrate load in a thiamine-depleted patient can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy — so thiamine/B vitamins are given before or with feeding.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.front: What blood tests make up a 'dementia screen' for reversible causes?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.back:
• TFTs
  • calcium
  • B12/folate
  • FBC
  • U&E
  • LFTs
  • glucose/HbA1c
  • CRP
— plus HIV and syphilis serology in at-risk patients.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.front: Name reversible/treatable contributors to cognitive decline the screen looks for.
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.back:
• Hypothyroidism
  • hypercalcaemia
  • B12/folate deficiency
  • and treatable infections (HIV, neurosyphilis)
— plus medication effects and alcohol.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.front: Which two conditions mimic dementia and must be excluded?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.back: Delirium (acute, fluctuating, often with an underlying cause) and depression ('pseudodementia').

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.front: What is the triad of normal-pressure hydrocephalus, and why does it matter?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.back: Dementia, gait apraxia and urinary incontinence ('wet, wobbly, wacky') — a reversible cause treatable with a shunt.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.front: What features of dementia warrant urgent/further investigation?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.back:
• Rapid progression
  • young onset
  • or focal neurology
— consider CJD, autoimmune encephalitis, or a structural lesion (imaging with CT/MRI).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.front: You find an unexplained raised CRP — what is the next step?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Me.back: Hunt for the source — blood and urine cultures, a CXR ± targeted imaging — and trend the CRP to monitor the response. Treat the patient clinically (e.g. Sepsis 6 if septic); don't wait for the level. Procalcitonin can help judge whether it's bacterial and when to stop antibiotics.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.question: A patient has a total calcium of 2.10 mmol/L (ref 2.20–2.60) and an albumin of 28 g/L. What is the corrected calcium and interpretation?
options: 2.34 mmol/L — normal (the low total was due to low albumin)
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.answer: 2.34 mmol/L — normal (the low total was due to low albumin)
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.explanation: Corrected Ca = 2.10 + 0.02 × (40 − 28) = 2.10 + 0.24 = 2.34 mmol/L, which is within the normal range. The low total calcium simply reflected hypoalbuminaemia — always correct before diagnosing hypocalcaemia.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.question: A 68-year-old with bone pain has an isolated raised ALP; calcium, phosphate and GGT are all normal. What does the normal GGT indicate about the source of the ALP?
options: A bony source (e.g. Paget's disease or osteomalacia)
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.answer: A bony source (e.g. Paget's disease or osteomalacia)
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.explanation: A normal GGT alongside a raised ALP points away from the liver and towards a bony source. In an older patient with bone pain and an isolated raised ALP, Paget's disease is a classic cause.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.question: A patient has a corrected calcium of 3.2 mmol/L with confusion and dehydration. What is the immediate management priority?
options: Reassurance and repeat in a week
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.explanation: Corrected calcium >3.0 mmol/L with symptoms is a hypercalcaemic emergency. The first step is aggressive IV saline rehydration; then treat the cause (commonly malignancy or primary hyperparathyroidism), with bisphosphonates as needed.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.question: Which statement about albumin in the bone profile is correct?
options: A high albumin causes true hypocalcaemia
A low albumin raises the corrected calcium falsely
A low albumin lowers the total calcium but not the ionised (active) calcium
Albumin does not affect calcium measurement
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.answer: A low albumin lowers the total calcium but not the ionised (active) calcium
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.explanation: About half of serum calcium is albumin-bound. A low albumin reduces the measured total calcium while the physiologically active ionised fraction is unchanged — hence the need to correct for albumin.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.question: An asymptomatic 60-year-old has a corrected calcium of 2.85 mmol/L with a PTH at the upper end of normal and a low phosphate. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.explanation: Hypercalcaemia with a PTH that is not suppressed (inappropriately normal or high) is primary hyperparathyroidism — the commonest cause of hypercalcaemia in ambulant outpatients. The low phosphate fits PTH excess.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.question: A patient with known metastatic breast cancer has a corrected calcium of 3.1 mmol/L. Which PTH result would you expect, and what is the mechanism?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.explanation: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy is PTH-independent (PTHrP secretion or osteolytic mets), so the parathyroid glands appropriately suppress and the PTH is low.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.question: A patient has mild hypercalcaemia with an inappropriately normal PTH, but a 24-hour urine shows a LOW urinary calcium (low calcium:creatinine clearance ratio). What is the diagnosis and key implication?
options: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (FHH) — avoid unnecessary surgery
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.answer: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (FHH) — avoid unnecessary surgery
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.explanation: FHH mimics primary hyperparathyroidism biochemically but has low urinary calcium excretion. It is benign, so distinguishing it prevents an unnecessary parathyroidectomy.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.question: A post-thyroidectomy patient has persistent hypocalcaemia despite IV calcium. Which additional electrolyte must be checked and corrected?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.explanation: Severe hypomagnesaemia causes functional hypoparathyroidism and impairs PTH action, so hypocalcaemia is refractory until the magnesium is replaced.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.question: A 68-year-old woman sustains a fragility wrist fracture. Calcium, phosphate, ALP and PTH are all normal. What is the most likely diagnosis and confirmatory test?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.explanation: A fragility fracture with an entirely normal bone profile is characteristic of osteoporosis, which is diagnosed on DEXA (T-score ≤ −2.5). Normal bloods help exclude secondary causes.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.question: An older adult with bone pain and proximal muscle weakness has ↓Ca, ↓PO₄, ↑ALP, ↑PTH and a low vitamin D. What is the diagnosis?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.explanation: Low calcium and phosphate with a raised ALP and PTH and low vitamin D is the secondary-hyperparathyroidism pattern of osteomalacia (vitamin D deficiency). Proximal myopathy and Looser's zones support it.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.question: An asymptomatic 75-year-old has an isolated ALP of 620 U/L with a normal calcium, phosphate and GGT. He mentions increasing hat size and hearing loss. What is the diagnosis?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.explanation: An isolated, markedly raised ALP with normal calcium/phosphate and a normal GGT (excluding a hepatic source), plus skull enlargement and deafness, is classic Paget's disease. Confirm with X-ray/isotope bone scan.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.question: A 70-year-old with back pain has hypercalcaemia, anaemia and renal impairment, but a NORMAL ALP. Which diagnosis should be actively excluded?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.explanation: Hypercalcaemia, anaemia and renal impairment with bone pain but a NORMAL ALP points to myeloma — its lytic lesions are osteoclastic with no osteoblastic (ALP) response. Send serum/urine electrophoresis and free light chains.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.question: A patient has low calcium, low phosphate, a raised ALP and raised PTH, with a low 25-OH vitamin D (osteomalacia). What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Replace vitamin D and recheck the bone profile
Arrange a DEXA scan to confirm
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.answer: Replace vitamin D and recheck the bone profile
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Cal.explanation: This biochemistry is vitamin D deficiency / osteomalacia (low Ca and phosphate, raised ALP, secondary hyperparathyroidism). Treatment is vitamin D replacement (± calcium); the bone profile normalises with treatment. Bisphosphonates are for osteoporosis/Paget's, and IV calcium is only for acute symptomatic hypocalcaemia.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.question: A dehydrated patient has urea 18 mmol/L with a creatinine of 95 µmol/L (only mildly raised). What does this urea:creatinine pattern indicate?
options: A pre-renal picture (e.g. dehydration or an upper GI bleed)
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.answer: A pre-renal picture (e.g. dehydration or an upper GI bleed)
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.explanation: Urea rising disproportionately to creatinine gives a high urea:creatinine ratio — a pre-renal pattern from dehydration/hypovolaemia, or an upper GI bleed where absorbed protein raises the urea.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.question: A patient has a potassium of 6.9 mmol/L with tall tented T waves on the ECG. What is the FIRST drug to give?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.explanation: With ECG changes, IV calcium gluconate is given first to stabilise the myocardium (cardioprotection). It does not lower potassium — insulin/dextrose and salbutamol are then used to shift K⁺ into cells.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.question: A well patient's routine bloods show K⁺ 6.5 mmol/L, but the sample was noted to be haemolysed and there are no ECG changes or clinical features. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Repeat the sample (pseudohyperkalaemia from haemolysis is likely)
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.answer: Repeat the sample (pseudohyperkalaemia from haemolysis is likely)
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.explanation: Haemolysis releases intracellular potassium and falsely raises the result. In a well patient with no ECG changes, repeat the sample — but never delay treating a genuinely high potassium with ECG changes.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.question: Which finding is characteristic of hypokalaemia on the ECG?
options: U waves and flattened T waves
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.answer: U waves and flattened T waves
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.explanation: Hypokalaemia flattens the T waves and produces U waves (and can prolong the QT). Tall tented T waves and a widened QRS are features of hyperkalaemia.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.question: An acutely septic, hypotensive patient has an eGFR reported as 22 mL/min/1.73m². Their creatinine was normal last month. How should this eGFR be interpreted?
options: Repeat the eGFR in 3 months to stage CKD
The eGFR confirms end-stage kidney disease
eGFR is invalid here — this is likely AKI, as creatinine is not in steady state
They need immediate dialysis based on the eGFR
They have established CKD stage G4
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.answer: eGFR is invalid here — this is likely AKI, as creatinine is not in steady state
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.explanation: eGFR assumes a steady-state creatinine. In acute illness with a rising creatinine it is invalid and this picture represents AKI, not CKD. Follow the creatinine trend and treat the acute cause.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.question: A patient has a stable eGFR of 40 mL/min/1.73m² and an ACR of 45 mg/mmol confirmed over 4 months. How is this classified?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.explanation: An eGFR of 40 falls in G3b (30–44) and an ACR >30 is A3. Persisting >3 months, this is CKD stage G3b A3 — a high-risk (KDIGO red) category needing close monitoring and optimisation.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.question: Which is the minimum duration of abnormality required to diagnose chronic (rather than acute) kidney disease?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.explanation: CKD requires a reduced GFR or markers of kidney damage present for at least 3 months, distinguishing it from acute kidney injury.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.question: A patient's creatinine rises from 90 to 120 µmol/L over 36 hours. Does this meet the KDIGO definition of AKI?
options: Only if urine output is also low
Yes — a rise of ≥26 µmol/L within 48 hours meets the definition
No — the rise is too small
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.answer: Yes — a rise of ≥26 µmol/L within 48 hours meets the definition
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.explanation: A creatinine rise of ≥26 µmol/L within 48 h (here 30) meets KDIGO stage 1 AKI, independent of urine output.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.question: An oliguric AKI patient has a potassium of 7.2 mmol/L that is not responding to medical therapy, with a severe metabolic acidosis. What is the appropriate escalation?
options: Give a further dose of oral calcium resonium and wait
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.explanation: Refractory hyperkalaemia and severe acidosis (two of the AEIOU indications) not responding to medical management require urgent dialysis.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.question: An elderly man with AKI has a palpable bladder and no urine output. What is the most important immediate investigation/action?
options: Catheterise and arrange a renal tract ultrasound to exclude obstruction
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.answer: Catheterise and arrange a renal tract ultrasound to exclude obstruction
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.explanation: A palpable bladder with anuria suggests post-renal (obstructive) AKI. Catheterisation may be immediately therapeutic, and ultrasound confirms/excludes obstruction (hydronephrosis) — a reversible cause.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.question: A euvolaemic patient has Na⁺ 122 mmol/L, low serum osmolality, urine osmolality 450 mosmol/kg, urine Na 45 mmol/L, with normal thyroid and cortisol. What is the diagnosis?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.explanation: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with a low serum osmolality but inappropriately concentrated urine (osm >100, urine Na >30) and normal thyroid/adrenal function is SIADH. Treat with fluid restriction.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.question: A patient with chronic hyponatraemia (Na 116) is corrected rapidly by 18 mmol/L over 24 hours and days later develops dysarthria, quadriparesis and a reduced conscious level. What has most likely happened?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.explanation: Over-rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia (>8–10 mmol/L/24 h) causes osmotic demyelination — a delayed, often irreversible syndrome. Sodium must be raised slowly with frequent monitoring.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.question: A dehydrated patient (dry, tachycardic, postural drop) has hyponatraemia with a urine sodium of 10 mmol/L. What does this suggest?
options: Hypovolaemic hyponatraemia with appropriate renal sodium retention (extrarenal loss)
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.answer: Hypovolaemic hyponatraemia with appropriate renal sodium retention (extrarenal loss)
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.explanation: A low urine sodium (<20) in a hypovolaemic patient indicates the kidney is appropriately conserving sodium — pointing to extrarenal fluid loss (e.g. D&V). A high urine Na would suggest renal loss (diuretics, Addison's).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.question: A patient with a red, hot, swollen first MTP joint has a serum urate that is within the normal range. What is the correct interpretation?
options: A normal urate does not exclude gout — urate often falls during an acute attack
Repeat the urate in 24 hours to confirm
Gout is excluded by the normal urate
The joint pain must be septic arthritis
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.answer: A normal urate does not exclude gout — urate often falls during an acute attack
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.explanation: Serum urate frequently drops into the normal range during an acute gout flare, so it cannot exclude the diagnosis. Confirm with joint aspiration (negatively birefringent MSU crystals) and recheck urate weeks later.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.question: 48 hours after starting chemotherapy for a high-grade lymphoma, a patient has a rising urate, K⁺ 6.3, high phosphate, low calcium and rising creatinine. What is the key urate-directed treatment?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.explanation: This is tumour lysis syndrome. Rasburicase rapidly breaks down urate and, with aggressive IV hydration, protects the kidneys; electrolytes (K⁺, phosphate, calcium) and renal function are monitored and managed.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.question: A 70-year-old with a hot, swollen knee and fever has a raised serum urate. What is the most important immediate step?
options: Request a serum urate in 6 weeks
Aspirate the joint for crystals AND Gram stain/culture to exclude septic arthritis
Start oral antibiotics empirically without aspiration
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.answer: Aspirate the joint for crystals AND Gram stain/culture to exclude septic arthritis
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.explanation: A hot, swollen joint with fever is septic arthritis until proven otherwise. A raised urate does not confirm gout — joint aspiration for crystals and microbiology is essential before assuming a crystal arthropathy.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.question: A patient's potassium of 2.7 mmol/L keeps returning low despite oral and IV potassium replacement. What is the key additional step?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & El.explanation: Coexisting hypomagnesaemia prevents potassium replacement from working (magnesium is needed for renal potassium handling), causing refractory hypokalaemia — check and correct it. Calcium gluconate, insulin/dextrose and salbutamol are treatments for HYPERkalaemia.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.question: A patient with a long alcohol history has AST 210, ALT 95, ALP 120, GGT very high. What pattern is this and what does the enzyme ratio suggest?
options: Hepatocellular pattern with AST:ALT >2 — suggestive of alcoholic liver disease
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.answer: Hepatocellular pattern with AST:ALT >2 — suggestive of alcoholic liver disease
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.explanation: ALT/AST rise predominates over ALP (hepatocellular), and an AST:ALT ratio >2 is characteristic of alcoholic liver disease.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.question: A jaundiced patient has ALP 640, GGT 480, ALT 70, with dark urine and pale stools. What pattern and category is this?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.explanation: A marked ALP/GGT rise out of proportion to ALT, with dark urine and pale stools, is an obstructive cholestatic picture (conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.question: A well 22-year-old has an isolated raised bilirubin (mostly unconjugated) with normal ALT, ALP and a normal blood film; it rises when he is unwell or fasting. What is the diagnosis?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.explanation: An isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with normal LFTs and no haemolysis, exacerbated by fasting/illness, is Gilbert's syndrome — benign and needs no treatment.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.question: A patient with a paracetamol overdose becomes jaundiced with an INR of 2.4 and new confusion. What does this indicate?
options: Acute liver failure — discuss urgently with a liver unit
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.answer: Acute liver failure — discuss urgently with a liver unit
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.explanation: Jaundice with coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5) and encephalopathy defines acute liver failure. Paracetamol is the commonest UK cause; give N-acetylcysteine and involve a liver/transplant unit early.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.question: A patient presents 3 days after the onset of severe epigastric pain. Amylase is normal. What is the best next test to assess for pancreatitis?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.explanation: Amylase falls within 24–48 h, so it can be normal in a late presentation. Lipase stays elevated longer and is more sensitive/specific — the better test here.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.question: A patient has confirmed acute pancreatitis with an amylase of 2000 U/L. How should severity be assessed?
options: With a validated score (Glasgow/APACHE II) and CRP — the amylase does not reflect severity
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.answer: With a validated score (Glasgow/APACHE II) and CRP — the amylase does not reflect severity
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.explanation: The magnitude of the amylase rise does not correlate with severity. Use a validated scoring system and CRP to stratify risk.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.question: A patient has a very high amylase but a CT abdomen shows a perforated duodenal ulcer and a normal pancreas. What does this illustrate?
options: Amylase is specific to the pancreas
A raised amylase is non-specific and occurs in other intra-abdominal pathology (e.g. perforation)
Amylase is more specific than lipase
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.answer: A raised amylase is non-specific and occurs in other intra-abdominal pathology (e.g. perforation)
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.explanation: Amylase is not pancreas-specific — bowel perforation/ischaemia, ectopic pregnancy, DKA and parotitis can all raise it. Correlate with the clinical picture and imaging.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.question: A cirrhotic patient becomes drowsy and confused; he is constipated and has a UTI. His ammonia is mildly raised. What is the best management approach?
options: Diagnosis depends on the ammonia level being very high
Treat the precipitants (constipation, infection) and give lactulose — HE is a clinical diagnosis
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.answer: Treat the precipitants (constipation, infection) and give lactulose — HE is a clinical diagnosis
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.explanation: Hepatic encephalopathy is diagnosed clinically; the ammonia correlates poorly with grade. Management is to identify and treat precipitants and give lactulose (± rifaximin).

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.question: A neonate becomes encephalopathic with a markedly raised ammonia but normal LFTs and no liver failure. What class of condition should be suspected?
options: An inborn error of metabolism (e.g. a urea cycle disorder)
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.answer: An inborn error of metabolism (e.g. a urea cycle disorder)
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.explanation: Hyperammonaemic encephalopathy in a neonate with normal liver function points to an inborn error of metabolism such as a urea cycle disorder — a metabolic emergency.

investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.question: A patient on sodium valproate develops confusion with a raised ammonia but normal LFTs. What is the likely mechanism?
investigations__BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pa.explanation: Valproate can cause hyperammonaemic encephalopathy independent of liver failure; stopping the drug (± carnitine) reverses it.
